name: Content calendar
summary: Know what goes out this week and who is holding it up. One row per piece with a status, an owner, a reviewer and a publish date, plus campaigns, key dates and a weekly editorial routine.
description: Posts, newsletters and videos slip when plans live in different documents and nobody knows who is reviewing what. This template sets up an editorial calendar for blog, newsletter, social and video: seven statuses from idea to published, a publishing calendar, a content pillar per piece, a disclosure check for paid or gifted content and a results check after 30 days. It fits creators, in-house marketers and agencies. It plans and tracks; it does not publish.

page.metaTitle: Content Calendar Template: Plan, Review, Publish
page.metaDescription: A content calendar template your AI agent builds in your CRM: owner, reviewer and publish date per piece, plus campaigns, key dates and a weekly routine.
page.headline: A content calendar template that shows who is holding up what, built by your AI agent
page.answer: A content calendar lists every post, newsletter and video with a status, an owner, a reviewer and a publish date, so you can see what goes out this week. Paste this template into your AI agent and it builds the calendar in Customermates, with campaigns, key dates, a disclosure check and a weekly editorial routine. It plans and tracks; it does not publish. You approve the plan before anything is built.

routine.title: The weekly 15-minute editorial meeting
steps: Go through what shipped last week and record the link to each published piece.
Look at what is due in the next 7 days and is not yet approved or scheduled: push it, cut it or rush it.
For every blocked piece, name who can unblock it and by when. A piece that has not moved for 14 days is unblocked or killed.
At the start of each month plan the next one: fill the slots to about 70 to 85 percent of capacity and keep two or three replacement pieces ready.

limits: It plans and tracks; it does not publish or schedule posts. Your publishing tool or CMS does that and reads the analytics, and the template never posts by itself.
It does not collect analytics. Reach, engagements and clicks are typed in or imported, and there is no link shortener or UTM builder.
It is not a design tool or an asset library. Images and video stay in your design tool, and the calendar keeps the link.
Approval is a recorded decision, not a legal sign-off or an audit trail for regulated content. Regulated industries keep their own compliance system.
Keep unpublished confidential copy, embargoed material, audience contact data and social account passwords out of it.
Reminders come from automation rules and notifications, or from a routine your agent runs on a schedule. The template proposes them and you decide which ones to switch on.

faq.question: What should a content calendar include?
faq.answer: Ten columns do most of the work: publish date, status, title, channel, format, owner, a link to the brief, the published URL, a pillar or campaign and the result after 30 days. Add a reviewer and a review date once more than one person is involved.

faq.question: How far ahead should I plan?
faq.answer: Plan 2 to 4 weeks ahead in detail, keep the month and the quarter in outline, and meet for 15 minutes each week. HubSpot's German guide suggests a rolling horizon of two to four weeks and a weekly editorial meeting for the next 7 to 14 days.

faq.question: Do I need to label paid or gifted content?
faq.answer: Usually yes, and rules differ by country, so check yours. In the US the FTC expects the disclosure with the endorsement, in plain words such as ad or sponsored, not buried among hashtags, and in both audio and text for video. The template has a disclosure field and a review step for paid or gifted pieces. This is not legal advice.

faq.question: Should a content calendar be a spreadsheet or a CRM?
faq.answer: A spreadsheet works for one person with one channel. Once people, brands and campaigns need to be linked, a review has a deadline and a published piece should trigger a follow-up task, a CRM keeps those as records instead of columns. The template does that and leaves publishing to your publishing tool.

faq.question: How many pieces should one person have in flight?
faq.answer: Rework suggests a cap of six per person (two drafting, two in review, two scheduled) and a kill rule for anything that has not moved for 14 days. Bitrix24 uses three for a writer, five for an editor and six for a manager. The template keeps the cap as a rule for the weekly meeting, not as a system limit.

faq.question: Can the agent publish for me?
faq.answer: No. The template plans and tracks; your publishing tool or CMS publishes. The prompt tells the agent to create no sample records.
